summary: Defines a human-readable text form for LDAP search filters. It replaces RFC 1960 and was replaced by RFCs 4510 and 4515.

plainLanguage.summary: A search filter is a question like find all people named Smith. This explains how to write such a question as a line of text.

questions: how to write an ldap filter
how to escape special characters in ldap filter
what does ldap filter ampersand mean
subtitle: A compact, human-readable text notation for LDAP search filters, such as (&(objectClass=Person)(sn=Jensen)).

tldr.problem: LDAP sends search filters over the network in a binary form, but applications and people also want a common way to write a filter as text.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a prefix-notation grammar in which each filter sits in parentheses, with & for and, | for or, ! for not, and a backslash-plus-two-hex-digits escape for special characters.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2254 replaced RFC 1960 and added LDAP version 3 extended match filters. It has since been replaced by RFC 4510 and RFC 4515.

today: RFC 2254 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4510 and RFC 4515, and it was updated by RFC 3377. It replaced RFC 1960.

sections.title: Why a Text Form for Filters
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) defines a network representation of a search filter that a client sends to an LDAP server. Some applications find it useful to have a common way of writing these filters in a human-readable form. This RFC defines that string format.

It replaces RFC 1960. The new text extends the string filter definition to cover LDAP version 3 extended match filters, and it can represent the full range of possible LDAP search filters.

The RFC carries an IESG note warning that update access in LDAPv3 lacks a mandatory authentication mechanism. Implementors were discouraged from deploying the update functionality until one was standardized.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers send questions to a phone book in a secret code. This RFC gives everyone a plain-writing way to say the same question, so people and programs can share it.

sections.title: The Filter Behind the Text
sections.content:
Section 4.5.1 of the LDAPv3 specification (RFC 2251) defines a Filter as a choice of ten forms: and, or, not, equalityMatch, substrings, greaterOrEqual, lessOrEqual, present, approxMatch and extensibleMatch.

Strings in a filter are limited to the UTF-8 encoding of the ISO 10646 character set. On the wire the filter is encoded with the Basic Encoding Rules, with simplifications described in the LDAP specification. The string form in this RFC is a text spelling of the same structure.
sections.plainLanguage: Underneath, a filter is built from a few kinds of building block, like and, or, not and "equals". The text form just gives each block a written symbol.

sections.title: The String Grammar
sections.content:
The string form follows ABNF and uses prefix notation: the operator comes first. Every filter is wrapped in parentheses. A filter is "(" filtercomp ")", and a component is an and, or, not or a single item.

  • & followed by one or more filters means and.
  • | followed by one or more filters means or.
  • ! followed by one filter means not.
  • An item compares an attribute with a value using = (equal), ~= (approximate), >= (greater) or <= (less).

An item can also be a presence test written attr=*, a substring match such as attr=initial*any*final, or an extensible match. The extensible form is attr [":dn"] [":" matchingrule] ":=" value, or the same without the attribute name. The RFC notes that although both the substring and present rules can produce attr=*, that text is used only to denote a presence filter.
sections.plainLanguage: You wrap every test in brackets and put the joining word first. "And" is an ampersand, "or" is an upright bar and "not" is an exclamation mark.

sections.title: Escaping Special Characters
sections.content:
If a value contains an asterisk (0x2a), an opening parenthesis (0x28), a closing parenthesis (0x29), a backslash (0x5c) or NUL (0x00), the character must be written as a backslash followed by two hexadecimal digits giving its ASCII value. The case of the hex digits is not significant.

This removes parsing ambiguity and lets any filter that LDAP can represent be written as a NUL-terminated string. Other characters, such as non-printing ones, may be escaped the same way. For example, a check for a cn value containing a literal asterisk is written (cn=*\2a*).
sections.plainLanguage: Some symbols already mean something in a filter, like brackets. To use one as plain text, you write a backslash and a short code for it, like putting a character in a costume so nobody mistakes it.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives simple filters such as (cn=Babs Jensen), (!(cn=Tim Howes)) and (o=univ*of*mich*). A combined one is (&(objectClass=Person)(|(sn=Jensen)(cn=Babs J*))), which matches person entries whose surname is Jensen or whose common name starts with "Babs J".

For extensible matching, (sn:dn:2.4.6.8.10:=Barney Rubble) uses matching rule 2.4.6.8.10 and also treats the attributes in an entry's distinguished name as part of the entry. Leaving the attribute off, as in (:dn:2.4.6.8.10:=Dino), applies the rule to any attribute that supports it.

Escaping examples include (o=Parens R Us \28for all your parenthetical needs\29) and (bin=\00\00\00\04), which searches for the four-byte value 0x00000004. Non-ASCII UTF-8 characters can be escaped byte by byte, as in (sn=Lu\c4\8di\c4\87).
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show real questions, like "find a person called Babs Jensen", and how to write a bracket or a star when you mean it as an ordinary letter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the string representation itself has no known security implications. LDAP search filters do, because LDAP servers interpret them to select the entries from which data is retrieved. Servers should therefore take care to protect the data they maintain from unauthorized access.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing the question down is harmless. The real care is needed by whoever holds the answers: they must not hand private information to just anyone.

viz.caption: CORE OF THE STRING FILTER GRAMMAR (RFC 2254, SECTION 4)

data.title: ABNF for string filters
data.code:
filter     = "(" filtercomp ")"
filtercomp = and / or / not / item
and        = "&" filterlist
or         = "|" filterlist
not        = "!" filter
filterlist = 1*filter
item       = simple / present / substring / extensible
simple     = attr filtertype value
filtertype = equal / approx / greater / less
equal      = "="
approx     = "~="
greater    = ">="
less       = "<="
present    = attr "=*"
